title: Greetings & Introductions
objectives: Greet people formally and informally
Introduce yourself by name
Use Austrian-specific greetings like Servus and Grüß Gott

grammar.explanation: German has formal (Sie) and informal (du) 'you'. In Tirol, locals are very friendly and often jump to 'du' fast — but use 'Sie' first with strangers, older people, and in shops.

examples.de: Wie heißen Sie?
examples.en: What is your name? (formal)

examples.de: Wie heißt du?
examples.en: What is your name? (informal)

examples.de: Grüß Gott! Ich heiße Bruck.
examples.en: Hello! My name is Bruck.

culturalNote: In Tirol locals shift to 'du' fast, but use 'Sie' first in shops and with strangers. Grüß Gott and Servus are more Austrian than German.

title: Numbers 1–20
objectives: Count from 1 to 20 in German
Understand the reversed structure of compound numbers (21–99)

grammar.explanation: Numbers 21–99 are 'backwards' in German: 21 = einundzwanzig = 'one and twenty'. Same in Tyrolean dialect, just sounds different.

examples.de: einundzwanzig
examples.en: 21 (one-and-twenty)

examples.de: dreiunddreißig
examples.en: 33 (three-and-thirty)

examples.de: Ich bin dreißig Jahre alt.
examples.en: I am thirty years old.

title: Ordering Food & Drink
objectives: Order food and drinks at a café or restaurant
Ask for the bill in the Austrian way
Know the genders of common food nouns

grammar.explanation: German nouns have three genders: der (masc), die (fem), das (neut). You MUST learn the article with the noun. There is no shortcut.

examples.de: der Kaffee
examples.en: coffee (masculine)

examples.de: das Brot
examples.en: bread (neuter)

examples.de: Ich möchte ein Bier und die Rechnung, bitte.
examples.en: I would like a beer and the bill, please.

culturalNote: Zahlen, bitte is the Austrian way to ask for the bill — you'll hear it everywhere. Mahlzeit is used as a greeting around lunchtime, not just at the table.

title: Days, Time, Weather
objectives: Name the days of the week
Tell the time using 'halb' correctly
Describe basic weather conditions

grammar.explanation: To say time: 'Es ist drei Uhr' = It is three o'clock. 'Halb drei' = 2:30 (literally 'half three' — meaning halfway TO three). This trips up English speakers.

examples.de: Es ist drei Uhr.
examples.en: It is three o'clock.

examples.de: Halb drei.
examples.en: 2:30 (half way to three)

examples.de: Heute ist Montag und es schneit.
examples.en: Today is Monday and it is snowing.

culturalNote: Austrians say Samstag, not Sonnabend (common in northern Germany). Snow vocab is essential — Tirol gets a lot of it.

title: Getting Around Tirol
objectives: Ask where things are using 'Wo ist…?'
Name key transport options in Tirol
Give and understand basic directions

grammar.explanation: Question words: Wer (who), Was (what), Wo (where), Wann (when), Warum (why), Wie (how). All start with W. Easy to remember.

examples.de: Wo ist der Bahnhof?
examples.en: Where is the train station?

examples.de: Wann fährt der Bus?
examples.en: When does the bus leave?

examples.de: Wo ist die Bergbahn, bitte?
examples.en: Where is the cable car, please?

culturalNote: The Bergbahn (mountain cable car) is a key part of getting around Tirol year-round — skiing in winter, hiking in summer. Die Hütte is not just a hut, it's a mountain restaurant on the slopes.

title: Shopping & Prices
objectives: Ask how much something costs
Express that something is too expensive
Understand the accusative case for masculine nouns

grammar.explanation: The accusative case: when something is the object of a verb, masculine 'der' changes to 'den'. Die and das stay the same. Example: 'Ich kaufe den Apfel' (masc.) but 'Ich kaufe die Birne' (fem.) and 'Ich kaufe das Brot' (neut.).

examples.de: Ich kaufe den Apfel.
examples.en: I buy the apple. (masc. → den)

examples.de: Ich kaufe die Birne.
examples.en: I buy the pear. (fem. stays die)

examples.de: Wie viel kostet das? — Zu teuer. Haben Sie etwas Günstigeres?
examples.en: How much does that cost? — Too expensive. Do you have something cheaper?

culturalNote: Innsbruck's Markthalle is a great place to practice shopping German. Markets run on cash — have coins ready.

title: At the Hotel
objectives: Check in and check out at a hotel
Request room types and ask what's available
Use modal verbs (können, müssen) correctly

grammar.point: Modal verbs + infinitive at the end
grammar.explanation: Modal verbs: können (can), müssen (must), wollen (want), dürfen (may). They always pair with an infinitive at the end of the sentence. 'Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.' — I can speak German.

examples.de: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.
examples.en: I can speak German.

examples.de: Können Sie mir helfen?
examples.en: Can you help me?

examples.de: Ich möchte ein Doppelzimmer für zwei Nächte, bitte.
examples.en: I would like a double room for two nights, please.

culturalNote: Austrian hotels almost always include breakfast (Frühstück). If it's not mentioned, ask: 'Ist das Frühstück inklusive?'

title: Family & People
objectives: Name core family members in German
Use mein/meine (my) correctly with masculine and feminine nouns
Ask and answer basic questions about your family

grammar.explanation: Use 'mein' before masculine and neuter nouns, 'meine' before feminine nouns and all plurals. Mein Vater (masc.), mein Kind (neut.), but meine Mutter (fem.), meine Kinder (pl).

examples.de: mein Vater
examples.en: my father (masculine → mein)

examples.de: meine Mutter
examples.en: my mother (feminine → meine)

examples.de: Meine Familie wohnt in Tirol — mein Vater, meine Mutter und meine Schwester.
examples.en: My family lives in Tirol — my father, my mother and my sister.

culturalNote: Austrian families are close-knit. 'Oma' and 'Opa' are the everyday words for grandmother and grandfather — nobody says 'Großmutter' in real conversation.

title: Colors & Clothes
objectives: Name five core colors in German
Identify basic clothing items
Use 'tragen' to describe what someone is wearing

grammar.point: Adjective after 'ist' vs before a noun
grammar.explanation: After 'sein' (to be), adjectives take no ending: Die Jacke ist rot. Before a noun, they get an ending: eine rote Jacke. Start with the 'is' pattern — it's easier.

examples.de: Die Jacke ist blau.
examples.en: The jacket is blue. (no ending after ist)

examples.de: Ich trage eine blaue Jacke.
examples.en: I am wearing a blue jacket. (-e ending before noun)

examples.de: Ich trage eine schwarze Jacke und eine blaue Hose.
examples.en: I am wearing a black jacket and blue trousers.

culturalNote: The traditional Tracht (folk costume) in Tirol is black, white and red. Locals still wear Dirndl and Lederhosen at festivals — the real thing, not touristy.

title: At the Doctor & Pharmacy
objectives: Describe symptoms using body parts (head, stomach, arm, leg)
Say you are ill and ask for help
Find a pharmacy and ask for medication

grammar.explanation: German uses the dative to express feelings. 'Mir ist schlecht' literally means 'to me it is bad'. You're not the subject — the feeling is. Same pattern: 'Mir ist kalt' (I feel cold), 'Mir ist warm' (I feel warm).

examples.de: Mir ist schlecht.
examples.en: I feel sick / nauseous.

examples.de: Mir ist kalt.
examples.en: I feel cold.

examples.de: Mir ist schlecht und ich habe Kopfschmerzen. Wo ist die nächste Apotheke?
examples.en: I feel sick and I have a headache. Where is the nearest pharmacy?

culturalNote: Austrian pharmacies (Apotheken) are strict — prescription meds need a Rezept. For basics like painkillers, just ask at the counter. Look for the green cross sign.

title: Talking About Yourself
objectives: Say where you come from and what you do for work
Express how long you have been doing something using 'seit'
Talk about interests using 'gern'

grammar.explanation: Use 'seit' (since/for) with the present tense to describe something still ongoing. English uses past perfect — German doesn't. 'Ich wohne seit einem Jahr hier' = I have been living here for one year.

examples.de: Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren in Tirol.
examples.en: I have been living in Tirol for two years.

examples.de: Ich lerne seit sechs Monaten Deutsch.
examples.en: I have been learning German for six months.

examples.de: Ich komme aus Kanada und wohne seit einem Jahr in Tirol. Ich lerne gern Deutsch.
examples.en: I come from Canada and have been living in Tirol for one year. I like learning German.

culturalNote: Austrians love asking where you come from. Saying you're learning German and living in Tirol goes down well. Locals appreciate the effort — you'll get respect for trying.

title: Asking Questions & Clarifying
objectives: Ask follow-up questions with Wie lange, Wie oft, Was für
Say you don't understand and ask for clarification
Politely ask someone to repeat or slow down

grammar.explanation: You already know Wer, Was, Wo, Wann, Warum, Wie. Now add: Wie lange (how long), Wie oft (how often), Was für (what kind of). These combine existing question words with common words.

examples.de: Wie lange wohnst du hier?
examples.en: How long have you been living here?

examples.de: Wie oft gehst du ins Training?
examples.en: How often do you go to practice?

examples.de: Wie bitte? Ich verstehe nicht — können Sie das wiederholen?
examples.en: Pardon? I don't understand — can you repeat that?

culturalNote: Austrians are patient with learners. 'Wie bitte?' is the polite way to ask someone to repeat — saying 'Was?' alone sounds rude.

title: Months & Seasons
objectives: Name the four seasons in German
Know key months for Tirol (ski season, hiking season)
Use 'im' correctly with months and seasons

grammar.explanation: To say 'in' a season or month, use 'im' (= in dem, dative): im Winter, im Sommer, im Januar. Never 'in der' or 'in das' for time periods.

examples.de: Im Winter fahre ich Ski.
examples.en: In winter I go skiing.

examples.de: Im Juli ist es sehr warm.
examples.en: In July it is very warm.

examples.de: Im Winter fahre ich Ski, im Sommer gehe ich wandern.
examples.en: In winter I ski, in summer I go hiking.

culturalNote: Tirol has two peak seasons: winter (December–April, skiing) and summer (July–September, hiking). The shoulder seasons (May, November) are quieter — locals call this 'Zwischensaison'.

title: My Home
objectives: Describe your home using basic rooms and features
Use 'Es gibt' to say what exists
Use location words: neben, gegenüber

grammar.explanation: 'Es gibt' means 'there is/are'. It always takes the accusative case. Masculine 'ein' becomes 'einen': Es gibt einen Garten. But Es gibt eine Küche (fem) and Es gibt ein Badezimmer (neut) stay the same.

examples.de: Es gibt einen Garten.
examples.en: There is a garden. (masc. → einen)

examples.de: Es gibt eine Küche.
examples.en: There is a kitchen. (fem. stays eine)

examples.de: Ich wohne in einer ruhigen Wohnung. Es gibt eine Küche und ein Badezimmer.
examples.en: I live in a quiet apartment. There is a kitchen and a bathroom.

culturalNote: Many expats in Tirol rent Wohnungen (apartments) rather than Häuser. Rent can be high in Innsbruck — be ready to describe what you need clearly.

title: Daily Routine
objectives: Describe your daily routine using common verbs
Use separable verbs: aufstehen
Talk about when you do things

grammar.explanation: Some German verbs split: the prefix moves to the END of the sentence. 'Aufstehen' (to get up): Ich STEHE um 7 Uhr AUF. The 'auf' jumps to the end. This applies to many common verbs: aufstehen, anfangen, aufhören, einkaufen.

examples.de: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
examples.en: I get up at seven o'clock.

examples.de: Ich höre um 18 Uhr auf.
examples.en: I finish at six o'clock.

examples.de: Normalerweise stehe ich früh auf, frühstücke und gehe dann ins Training.
examples.en: Normally I get up early, have breakfast and then go to training.

culturalNote: Austrian work days often start early — 7am is common in trades. 'Feierabend' (end of the work day) is a beloved institution, usually around 5pm.

title: Deeper Restaurant German
objectives: Order elegantly using 'Ich hätte gern…'
Navigate a full menu: Vorspeise, Hauptspeise, Nachspeise
Handle dietary needs and ask about spice levels

grammar.explanation: 'Ich hätte gern' is the Konjunktiv II of 'haben' — polite and elegant. More natural than 'ich möchte' in nicer restaurants. Hätte = would have. Gern = gladly.

examples.de: Ich hätte gern das Tagesgericht.
examples.en: I'd like the dish of the day.

examples.de: Ich hätte gern die Rechnung.
examples.en: I'd like the bill.

examples.de: Ich hätte gern die Vorspeise und danach das Tagesgericht — ohne Zwiebeln, bitte.
examples.en: I'd like the starter and then the dish of the day — without onions, please.

culturalNote: Austrian restaurants often include a Tagesgericht (dish of the day) — usually the best value. Trinkgeld (tip) is not mandatory but rounding up 10% is expected.

title: Making Plans
objectives: Suggest activities using 'Hast du Lust…?' and 'Wollen wir…?'
Accept or decline invitations naturally
Use 'vielleicht', 'auf jeden Fall', 'Schade!'

grammar.explanation: To invite someone, use 'Hast du Lust, X zu tun?' — Do you feel like doing X? The 'zu' + infinitive construction is essential at A2. Wollen wir…? (Shall we…?) works similarly but without 'zu'.

examples.de: Hast du Lust, ins Kino zu gehen?
examples.en: Do you feel like going to the cinema?

examples.de: Wollen wir heute Ski fahren?
examples.en: Shall we go skiing today?

examples.de: Hast du Lust, heute Abend in die Hütte zu gehen? — Ich bin dabei! Wann passt es dir?
examples.en: Do you feel like going to the mountain hut tonight? — Count me in! When works for you?

culturalNote: Austrians tend to plan things fairly last-minute. 'Vielleicht' often means 'probably not'. 'Auf jeden Fall' means they're actually coming.

title: Past Tense — Perfekt
objectives: Form the Perfekt tense using haben + Partizip II
Know which verbs use 'sein' instead of 'haben'
Use gestern and letzte Woche in sentences

grammar.explanation: German speech mostly uses the Perfekt (not Präteritum) for the past. Formula: auxiliary verb (haben or sein) in position 2, Partizip II at the END. Most verbs use 'haben'. Motion and change-of-state verbs use 'sein': Ich BIN gegangen (not 'habe').

examples.de: Ich habe Kaffee getrunken.
examples.en: I drank coffee. (haben + participle)

examples.de: Ich bin ins Büro gegangen.
examples.en: I went to the office. (sein + motion verb)

examples.de: Gestern habe ich gut gespielt — kein Gegentor! Ich bin danach in die Hütte gegangen.
examples.en: Yesterday I played well — no goals conceded! Afterwards I went to the mountain hut.

culturalNote: In spoken Austrian German, Präteritum (I went, I did) is almost never used except for sein/haben/modals. Always use Perfekt in conversation.

title: Working Life
objectives: Talk about your workplace and colleagues
Use separable verbs anfangen and aufhören
Describe a work day using Perfekt

grammar.explanation: Recall: separable verbs split when conjugated — prefix goes to end. Anfangen (to start): Die Besprechung FÄNGT um 9 AN. Aufhören (to stop): Ich HÖRE um 17 Uhr AUF. Note the irregular 'fängt' — irregular stem change from 'fangen'.

examples.de: Die Besprechung fängt um neun an.
examples.en: The meeting starts at nine.

examples.de: Wann hörst du heute auf?
examples.en: When do you finish today?

examples.de: Ich fange um acht an, arbeite von Zuhause und höre um fünf auf. Endlich Feierabend!
examples.en: I start at eight, work from home and finish at five. Finally done for the day!

culturalNote: 'Feierabend' is one of those untranslatable German words — it's the feeling of freedom when the work day ends. Austrians take it seriously.

title: Expressing Opinions
objectives: Use 'meiner Meinung nach' and 'ich finde, dass…'
Agree and disagree politely
Use discourse connectors: einerseits, andererseits, übrigens

grammar.explanation: When you say 'I think that…', the 'dass' sends the verb to the end of the clause. 'Ich finde, dass Tirol SCHÖN IST' — not 'ist schön'. The verb comes last after 'dass', 'weil', 'obwohl' and most subordinating conjunctions.

examples.de: Ich finde, dass Tirol wunderschön ist.
examples.en: I think that Tirol is beautiful.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass das zu teuer ist.
examples.en: I think that's too expensive.

examples.de: Meiner Meinung nach ist TypeScript besser als JavaScript — ich finde, dass das strenge Typsystem sehr hilfreich ist.
examples.en: In my opinion TypeScript is better than JavaScript — I think the strict type system is very helpful.

culturalNote: Austrian debate culture tends to be indirect. Use softeners like 'Ich würde sagen…' or 'Ehrlich gesagt…' — blunt opinions can sound aggressive.

title: Conditionals & Hypotheticals
objectives: Use wenn-clauses for real conditions
Use Konjunktiv II (würde, hätte) for hypotheticals
Connect sentences with obwohl, trotzdem, deshalb

grammar.explanation: For wishes and hypotheticals, use 'würde' + infinitive at the end. 'Ich würde gern nach Wien fahren' = I would like to go to Vienna. For conditions: 'Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich jeden Tag trainieren.' — hätte is Konjunktiv II of haben.

examples.de: Ich würde gern mehr Deutsch lernen.
examples.en: I would like to learn more German.

examples.de: Wenn ich in Kanada wäre, würde ich Eishockey spielen.
examples.en: If I were in Canada, I would play ice hockey.

examples.de: Wenn es morgen schneit, würde ich gern Ski fahren. Sonst gehe ich ins Training.
examples.en: If it snows tomorrow, I'd like to go skiing. Otherwise I'll go to practice.

culturalNote: Konjunktiv II is used constantly in polite Austrian speech — 'Hätten Sie…?', 'Könnte ich…?' Mastering it will make you sound much more natural.

title: Dative Prepositions
objectives: Recognise and use the 8 core dative prepositions
Master the contractions zum, zur, vom, beim
Build fluent location and direction phrases

grammar.explanation: These 8 prepositions ALWAYS take the dative: mit, bei, nach, von, seit, aus, zu, außer. Key contractions: zu + dem = zum, zu + der = zur, von + dem = vom, bei + dem = beim. Memorise these — they're everywhere.

examples.de: Ich gehe zum Bahnhof. (zu + dem = zum)
examples.en: I'm going to the train station.

examples.de: Ich komme vom Training. (von + dem = vom)
examples.en: I'm coming from practice.

examples.de: Ich fahre mit dem Bus zum Bahnhof, dann mit dem Zug nach Innsbruck.
examples.en: I take the bus to the train station, then the train to Innsbruck.

culturalNote: Getting your prepositions right will dramatically reduce the 'foreigner' feel. Locals notice when someone says 'zu dem Arzt' instead of 'zum Arzt'.

title: The Passive Voice
objectives: Form the passive with werden + Partizip II
Use 'man' as the active alternative
Describe what is allowed, forbidden, or required

grammar.explanation: To say something IS DONE (by someone/something), use: subject + werden + … + Partizip II. 'Das Bier wird kalt serviert' = The beer is served cold. Often replaced in speech by 'man': 'Man serviert das Bier kalt' — same meaning, more casual.

examples.de: Das Programm wird täglich benutzt.
examples.en: The program is used daily.

examples.de: Man darf hier nicht parken.
examples.en: You cannot park here.

examples.de: In Tirol wird viel Ski gefahren. Man sagt, dass der Schnee hier der beste ist.
examples.en: A lot of skiing is done in Tirol. They say the snow here is the best.

culturalNote: German bureaucratic language loves the passive. Signs, rules, and official notices are almost always in the passive — 'Es wird gebeten…' (You are requested to…).

title: Making Complaints
objectives: Complain politely using Konjunktiv II
Describe what's broken or not working
Request a solution or refund confidently

grammar.explanation: Direct complaints can sound aggressive. Soften with Konjunktiv II: 'Ich möchte mich beschweren' (I'd like to complain) or 'Ich hätte gerne eine Erstattung' (I'd like a refund). Adding 'bitte' always helps.

examples.de: Ich hätte gerne eine Erstattung, bitte.
examples.en: I'd like a refund, please.

examples.de: Das entspricht leider nicht meinen Erwartungen.
examples.en: Unfortunately that doesn't meet my expectations.

examples.de: Entschuldigung, das Gerät ist kaputt. Können Sie das bitte reparieren oder mir eine Erstattung geben?
examples.en: Excuse me, the device is broken. Can you please fix it or give me a refund?

culturalNote: Austrians tend to complain less directly than Germans. A calm, polite complaint with 'Konjunktiv II' will get better results than a direct demand. Start with 'Entschuldigung…'
